claims.judged: Does acute sleep deprivation impair reversal learning in mice?
If it does, is the impairment mediated by reduced orbitofrontal activity?
claims.text: Answered negatively, within the design's limits.

claims.judged: The project will not test chronic sleep restriction or human participants.
Acute (24 h) sleep deprivation impairs reversal learning in mice.
claims.text: r1 is a large, well-powered effect.

claims.judged: The impairment is mediated by reduced orbitofrontal cortex activity during reversal.
claims.text: r2 finds no difference; the paper correctly says so.

claims.judged: Sleep-deprived mice need more trials than controls to reach criterion after a reward-contingency reversal.
Sleep-deprived mice show fewer c-Fos-positive cells in orbitofrontal cortex after the reversal session.
claims.text: Not met; a null with reasonable power.

claims.judged: Two-choice odour discrimination with a single reward-contingency reversal; trials to criterion (8 of 10 correct) compared between 24 h sleep-deprived and rested
c-Fos immunostaining in lateral orbitofrontal cortex 90 min after the reversal session; positive-cell density compared between groups.
claims.text: No engagement control was added, as funding requested.

claims.judged: c-Fos density cannot distinguish reduced orbitofrontal activity from reduced task engagement; the design bears on prediction p2 only correlationally.
claims.text: The limit stands and is stated.

claims.judged: Sleep-deprived mice required 41 ± 6 trials to criterion after reversal versus 27 ± 4 for rested controls (n = 16 per group; d = 1.1; p < 0.001).
c-Fos-positive cell density in lateral orbitofrontal cortex did not differ between groups (312 ± 40 vs 298 ± 45 cells/mm²; p = 0.61).
claims.text: A clean null; power to detect a 20% difference was ~0.8.

claims.judged: Acute sleep deprivation impairs reversal learning without a detectable reduction in orbitofrontal activation, so the behavioural effect is unlikely to be mediat
claims.text: Correct as far as c-Fos goes; 'unlikely to be mediated' is stronger than a single correlational null allows.
The behavioural finding is solid and the negative mechanistic result is reported honestly; the interpretation should be softened.
